question: When did you first realize you wanted to pursue photography seriously, rather than just as a hobby?
lookingFor: A specific, credible moment or period that shows real engagement, not a vague love of pictures.

bullets: Name a concrete moment, project, or image that shifted things
Show the progression from casual interest to deliberate practice
Connect it to why you now want formal study
idealAnswer.modelAnswer: I'd been taking phone photos for years without thinking much of it, but it changed when I borrowed my uncle's old film camera for a school trip and got the roll developed to find half the shots were completely wrong exposures. That failure made me want to understand what I was actually doing instead of just pointing and shooting, so I started reading about exposure and composition and saving up for my own camera. Two years on I'm shooting most weekends, and I want formal training because I've hit the limit of what I can teach myself from tutorials.

commonMistakes: Saying photography has 'always' been a passion with no specific trigger
Describing only phone snapshots with no deliberate practice
Not connecting the origin story to why they want a degree now
followUps: What's changed in how you shoot since that first moment?

question: Why do you want to study Photography here specifically, rather than teaching yourself or doing a shorter course?
lookingFor: Specific knowledge of the course's strengths and a clear sense of what structured study gives them that self-teaching can't.

bullets: Name something specific about the course (facilities, tutors, curriculum structure)
Explain what self-teaching hasn't given them — critique, technical range, darkroom access
Show they've looked at the course beyond its prospectus page
idealAnswer.modelAnswer: I've taught myself the basics of digital shooting and editing over three years, but what I can't replicate alone is rigorous critique and access to a proper darkroom, and your course is one of the few that still runs analogue processing alongside digital modules. I looked at the final-year show from last year online and the range of approaches, from documentary to studio lighting work, told me the course pushes students to be technically broad rather than settle into one style early. I want that breadth before I specialize, and a short course wouldn't give me the year-long project time to actually develop a body of work.

commonMistakes: Generic praise that could apply to any photography course
Only mentioning equipment without addressing pedagogy or critique
Implying formal study is just a formality they don't really need
followUps: What would you want to get out of critique sessions specifically?

question: Talk us through one image in your portfolio you're proudest of, and one you'd now do differently.
lookingFor: Honest self-critique and technical vocabulary, showing growth rather than defending every choice.

bullets: Explain the intent and technical decisions behind the strong image
Give a genuine weaker image and identify precisely what's wrong
Show what they'd change and why, demonstrating growth
idealAnswer.modelAnswer: The one I'm proudest of is a portrait I shot using only window light and a reflector, where I waited nearly twenty minutes for the light to soften as clouds moved in, and the patience shows in how gentle the shadows are on her face. The one I'd redo is an early street shot where I underexposed the background to protect the highlights on my subject, but I lost too much shadow detail and it looks flat printed large. Now I'd bracket the exposure or shoot raw with more headroom, because at the time I didn't fully understand how much I could recover versus how much was gone for good.

commonMistakes: Only praising work with no genuine critique offered
Vague answers like 'I'd just make it better' with no technical specifics
Picking a weak image but not actually explaining what's technically wrong
followUps: How do you decide when an image is finished?

question: Which photographer's work has influenced you most, and what specifically have you taken from it?
lookingFor: Genuine familiarity with a photographer's actual work and a specific, articulable influence rather than a name-drop.

bullets: Name a photographer they can discuss with real detail
Point to specific images or a specific technique or theme
Explain concretely how it's shown up in their own work
idealAnswer.modelAnswer: Vivian Maier's street work is the one I keep going back to, particularly how she photographed strangers with such closeness and yet no sense of intrusion. What I've taken from her is the discipline of waiting for a genuine, unguarded moment rather than asking someone to pose, and I try to practice that on my own city walks even though I still find it uncomfortable to shoot strangers up close. Looking at contact sheets of hers that have been published, you can see she'd take dozens of frames of the same scene waiting for the right gesture, which taught me that patience matters more than luck.

commonMistakes: Naming a famous photographer with no specific knowledge of their work
Confusing photographers or misattributing images
No connection drawn between the influence and their own practice
followUps: Is there anything about their approach you'd push back on or do differently?

question: Can you explain the exposure triangle and how the three elements interact?
lookingFor: Solid grasp of aperture, shutter speed, and ISO, and how trading one off against another affects the image beyond just brightness.

bullets: Define aperture, shutter speed, and ISO and what each controls
Explain that they work together to reach a correct exposure
Note the secondary effect each has (depth of field, motion blur, noise)
idealAnswer.modelAnswer: The exposure triangle is aperture, shutter speed, and ISO, and together they determine how much light hits the sensor for a given shot. Aperture is the size of the lens opening, which controls light and also depth of field, so a wide aperture like f/1.8 lets in more light but blurs the background more. Shutter speed is how long the sensor is exposed, which affects light and motion blur, and ISO is the sensor's sensitivity, which brightens the image but adds noise at higher values. The skill is balancing all three for both the right exposure and the right look, not just getting a properly lit photo.

commonMistakes: Only naming the three terms without explaining the trade-offs
Confusing which setting controls depth of field versus motion blur
Treating ISO as free brightness with no mention of noise
followUps: If you wanted to freeze a fast-moving subject in low light, how would you adjust each setting?

question: What composition techniques do you rely on, and can you name a time breaking one improved a photo?
lookingFor: Working knowledge of composition principles plus the maturity to know they're guidelines, not laws.

bullets: Name specific techniques such as rule of thirds, leading lines, or framing
Give a real example from their own shooting
Describe a case where deliberately breaking a rule served the image
idealAnswer.modelAnswer: I default to the rule of thirds and leading lines most often, especially in landscape work where a road or riverbank can pull the eye through the frame. But for a portrait of my grandmother I centered her completely instead of off-setting her to a third, because the symmetry felt more like a formal, respectful sitting than a candid moment, and off-center would have undercut that. I think the rules are useful defaults for when you don't have a stronger reason to do something else, and knowing when you do have that reason is the actual skill.

commonMistakes: Reciting rules with no example from their own work
Treating composition rules as absolute laws that must never be broken
Vague claim of breaking rules with no specific justification
followUps: How do you decide where to place your subject in the frame before you shoot?

question: What do you see as the real differences between shooting film and digital, beyond convenience?
lookingFor: Understanding that goes beyond 'film is nostalgic' to real technical and workflow differences, ideally from hands-on experience.

bullets: Identify genuine technical differences (dynamic range, grain vs noise, latitude)
Discuss workflow differences such as cost per frame and shooting discipline
Avoid romanticizing film without acknowledging digital's strengths
idealAnswer.modelAnswer: Beyond the obvious cost and speed differences, I've found film forces a different discipline because you can't chimp the back of the camera, so you have to actually trust your metering and think harder before pressing the shutter. Color negative film also has a lot of exposure latitude, so I can overexpose by a couple of stops and still recover a usable image, which is different from digital where you're usually protecting highlights more carefully. That said, digital's dynamic range in raw files is now excellent and the ability to review and reshoot immediately is genuinely useful for controlled work like studio portraits, so I don't think one is simply better, they suit different situations.

commonMistakes: Reducing the difference purely to nostalgia or aesthetic trend
No evidence of actually having shot film
Dismissing digital as inferior with no acknowledgment of its strengths
followUps: Which would you choose for a paid client shoot, and why?

question: Which genre of photography draws you most right now, and why do you think that is?
lookingFor: A genuine, reasoned preference with self-awareness about why it fits them, not just a list of genres they've tried.

bullets: Name a specific genre with a clear reason for the pull
Reflect on what about their own personality or interests connects to it
Show openness to it evolving rather than treating it as fixed
idealAnswer.modelAnswer: Documentary work is what pulls me most right now, particularly photographing small local businesses in my town before they change hands or close. I think it's because I like the research side as much as the shooting, getting to know someone's story before I even lift the camera, and I find that patience produces more honest images than trying to catch a stranger cold. I know that might shift once I'm exposed to more genres on the course, but right now the combination of people and place is what keeps me shooting on days I don't have an assignment.

commonMistakes: Claiming to love every genre equally with no real preference
No self-reflection on why that genre specifically appeals to them
Treating the answer as permanently fixed with no openness to change
followUps: What genre do you feel weakest in, and how would you improve it?

question: How much post-processing do you think is acceptable, and where's the line for you personally?
lookingFor: A thought-out personal position on editing that distinguishes technical correction from misrepresentation, ideally tied to genre.

bullets: Distinguish between technical correction and content manipulation
Acknowledge the line shifts depending on genre (documentary vs conceptual)
Explain their own personal practice with reasoning
idealAnswer.modelAnswer: I think the acceptable amount depends heavily on genre. For documentary or photojournalistic work I'm strict with myself, I'll adjust exposure, contrast, and crop, but I won't remove or add elements because the whole point is representing what was actually there. For conceptual or fine art work I'm much more open to compositing and heavy manipulation because the image is announcing itself as constructed. Personally my line is honesty about intent, if a viewer would reasonably assume they're seeing an unaltered record of a moment, I hold myself to minimal editing.

commonMistakes: Treating all editing as equally acceptable regardless of genre
Refusing to edit at all, confusing minimal processing with no processing
No personal stance, just describing what software can do
followUps: Have you ever seen an edited image cross that line for you, and what was it?

question: How do you put a nervous or self-conscious subject at ease during a shoot?
lookingFor: Practical, specific techniques from real experience, showing the interpersonal side of photography isn't overlooked.

bullets: Give concrete techniques, not just 'I talk to them'
Show awareness that comfort directly affects image quality
Draw on a real experience where it worked or didn't
idealAnswer.modelAnswer: I usually start by shooting a few frames before I say anything about how they look, just to get them used to the sound of the shutter without the pressure of a countdown. I also give them something to do with their hands or a small task, like asking them to look at something specific off camera, because stillness with nothing to focus on is what makes people stiffen up. When I photographed my friend's mother for a family project, she kept apologizing for not smiling naturally, so I switched to asking her questions about her garden while I shot, and the change in her face was immediate.

commonMistakes: Vague answer like 'I just make them comfortable' with no technique
No acknowledgment that subject comfort affects the actual images
Describing only posing directions with no rapport-building
followUps: How does your approach change with children versus adults?

question: Where do you stand on photographing strangers in public without their consent?
lookingFor: Nuanced ethical reasoning that weighs legal rights against dignity and context, not a blanket rule.

bullets: Acknowledge the legal right versus the ethical question aren't the same thing
Weigh context, such as vulnerability of the subject and how the image will be used
Land on a personal working principle rather than refusing to take a position
idealAnswer.modelAnswer: Legally in most public places you can photograph strangers, but I don't think that settles whether you should, so I think about it case by case. If someone is in a vulnerable moment, grieving, or clearly wouldn't want to be seen that way, I'll usually not press the shutter or I'll delete it afterward, because the image isn't worth the harm. For more neutral street scenes, like someone reading on a bench, I'm more comfortable, especially if I'd be happy to show them the photo and explain why I took it. My working principle is roughly, would I be able to justify this to the person directly, and if the honest answer is no, I don't take the shot.

commonMistakes: Claiming a blanket 'anything legal is fine' position with no ethical reflection
Refusing street photography entirely without engaging with its documentary value
Confusing legal permission with ethical justification
followUps: Does your answer change if the subject is a public figure?

question: How would you describe the difference between hard and soft light, and when would you choose each?
lookingFor: Clear technical understanding of light quality and its practical application to mood and subject.

bullets: Define hard light (small/distant source, sharp shadows) versus soft light (large/close source, gradual shadows)
Give a genre or mood example for each
Mention a practical way to modify light between the two
idealAnswer.modelAnswer: Hard light comes from a small or distant source relative to the subject, like direct midday sun, and it creates sharp-edged, high-contrast shadows. Soft light comes from a larger or closer source, like an overcast sky or a diffuser, and the shadows fade gradually instead of cutting off sharply. I reach for hard light when I want drama or texture, like showing the lines on someone's hands in a documentary portrait, and soft light for most beauty or flattering portrait work because it's more forgiving on skin. A reflector or a shoot-through umbrella is usually how I soften a hard source when I don't have natural soft light available.

commonMistakes: Confusing hard and soft light with bright and dim light
No practical example of when each would be chosen
Not knowing any technique to modify light quality
followUps: What would you do if you only had harsh midday sun and needed a flattering portrait?

question: What camera and lenses do you currently shoot with, and why did you choose them?
lookingFor: Genuine hands-on familiarity with their own equipment and reasoned, not just brand-driven, choices.

bullets: Name actual equipment they use, showing real hands-on experience
Explain the reasoning behind the choice (budget, focal length, genre fit)
Show awareness of the gear's limitations
idealAnswer.modelAnswer: I shoot with a secondhand crop-sensor DSLR and mostly a 35mm equivalent prime lens, which I chose because it's close to how the eye naturally sees and forces me to move around rather than zoom. I picked it over a kit zoom lens once I'd saved enough because the wider aperture lets me shoot in lower light and gives a nicer background blur for portraits. Its main limitation is that I can't get close to distant subjects, so for anything further away I have to physically get nearer, which has actually made me a more deliberate shooter.

commonMistakes: No real familiarity with the gear they claim to use
Choosing gear purely by brand reputation with no functional reasoning
Not acknowledging any limitation of their current setup
followUps: If budget were no object, what would you add to your kit first?

question: Tell us about a personal photography project you've pursued over time. What did you learn from sustaining it?
lookingFor: Evidence of self-directed, sustained work beyond one-off assignments, and reflection on what long-term projects teach.

bullets: Describe a specific project with a clear concept and duration
Explain what kept them going or what made it hard to sustain
Reflect on how the work or their approach changed over the project's life
idealAnswer.modelAnswer: For about eight months I photographed the same barbershop near my house once a month, trying to capture the regulars and how the space changed with the seasons. The hardest part wasn't the shooting, it was staying disciplined enough to keep showing up on months when nothing seemed to be happening, and I learned that some of my strongest images came from those quiet, uneventful visits rather than anything dramatic. By the end my style had shifted from wide establishing shots to much tighter, quieter portraits, because I'd earned enough trust with the regulars to get close.

commonMistakes: Describing a single shoot as if it were a sustained project
No reflection on what changed in their approach over time
Vague project concept with no clear throughline
followUps: What would you do differently if you started that project again today?

question: Tell us about a time a shoot went technically wrong. How did you handle it?
lookingFor: A concrete failure with honest ownership and a practical response, showing composure under pressure.

bullets: Describe a genuine technical failure, not a minor inconvenience
Explain the in-the-moment decision they made to adapt
Reflect on what they changed afterward to prevent it recurring
idealAnswer.modelAnswer: I was shooting a friend's small event and my flash trigger stopped syncing halfway through, so half my frames from that stretch were unusable with black bands across them. In the moment I switched to available light and pushed my ISO higher than I'd normally like, accepting more grain in exchange for actually getting the shots. Afterward I started carrying a backup trigger and testing the whole kit the night before any booked shoot, because I realized I'd never actually stress-tested the gear beforehand, I'd just trusted it would work.

commonMistakes: Describing a trivial problem as if it were a serious failure
No real adaptation described, just recounting that it went wrong
No lasting change to their process afterward
followUps: What's in your kit now specifically because of a past failure?

question: What draws you to photography specifically, rather than painting, film, or graphic design?
lookingFor: A clear sense of what's unique to the photographic medium for them personally, not just a general love of images.

bullets: Identify something specific to photography's relationship with reality or time
Contrast it honestly with another visual medium they've also tried
Ground the answer in personal experience rather than abstract theory
idealAnswer.modelAnswer: I actually did painting for years before photography, and what pulled me away was that painting starts from nothing on a blank canvas, whereas photography starts from what's actually in front of you and the skill is in selection and timing rather than invention. I find that constraint more interesting, having to notice something rather than construct it from imagination. I also tried a bit of short filmmaking, but I prefer the single decisive frame over a sequence, there's something about having to say everything in one image that suits how I think.

commonMistakes: No real comparison, just stating they've always liked photos
Dismissing other visual arts as inferior rather than explaining personal fit
Answer with no evidence they've actually tried another medium
followUps: Is there anything from painting or another medium you still bring into your photography?

question: Have you read any photography criticism or theory? What's stayed with you from it?
lookingFor: Evidence of engagement with photographic thinking beyond technique, and ability to articulate an idea in their own words.

bullets: Name a specific text, writer, or idea they've actually engaged with
Explain the core idea in their own words, not just the title
Connect it to how it's changed how they look at or make images
idealAnswer.modelAnswer: I read Susan Sontag's On Photography for a school project and the idea that stuck with me was her argument that photographing something can substitute for actually experiencing it, which made me a lot more self-conscious about when I'm hiding behind the camera instead of being present. It made me change how I shoot at events I actually care about, I now put the camera down for stretches rather than shooting the whole time. I don't agree with everything in it, some of her argument feels dated given how differently images circulate now, but it's the book that first made me think of photography as something with an ethics, not just a technique.

commonMistakes: Naming a book or writer with no actual grasp of the argument
Reciting an idea with no personal reaction or disagreement
Claiming no exposure to any theory or criticism at all
followUps: Is there a point in that reading you'd actually disagree with?

question: How do you think AI image generation is affecting photography as a discipline, and how does it change what you want to study?
lookingFor: A considered, current view that distinguishes photography's evidentiary and craft value from generated imagery, without dismissing the topic.

bullets: Show awareness of the actual debate, not just a surface reaction
Distinguish what photography offers that generated imagery doesn't (indexical link to reality, lived process)
Connect it to their own reasons for wanting to study photography now
idealAnswer.modelAnswer: I think AI generation is going to devalue purely illustrative, stock-style imagery quickly, because a client who just needs a generic picture of a sunset doesn't need a photographer for that anymore. But it makes the things photography can uniquely do more valuable, the fact that a documentary image is evidence something actually happened in front of a lens, and that a portrait carries a real relationship between photographer and subject. If anything it's sharpened why I want to study this now, I want to be strong in the kind of work, documentary and portraiture built on real access and trust, that generated images fundamentally can't replace.

commonMistakes: Dismissing the question or claiming AI has no effect on the field
Pure alarmism with no reasoned distinction of what photography still offers
Not connecting the answer back to their own study plans
followUps: Do you see a place for AI tools in your own editing workflow?

question: Describe a time critique of your work stung, but turned out to be right. How did you respond?
lookingFor: Openness to critique and evidence of actually acting on feedback rather than just accepting it politely.

bullets: Describe genuine critical feedback, not a soft compliment
Be honest about the initial reaction before accepting it
Show the specific change made to their work afterward
idealAnswer.modelAnswer: A photography teacher once told me my landscape work was technically competent but emotionally empty, that I was photographing pretty views instead of actually saying anything, and it stung because I'd been proud of those images for their sharpness and exposure. I was defensive at first, but sitting with it I realized she was right, I'd been optimizing for technical correctness instead of asking what I wanted the image to communicate. Since then I try to write one sentence about what I want a shot to say before I take it, and my work has gotten more inconsistent technically but far more interesting to look at.

commonMistakes: Describing feedback that was actually just praise
No honest admission of an initial defensive reaction
No concrete change made as a result of the critique
followUps: How do you separate useful critique from feedback that's just a matter of taste?

question: What would you bring to critique sessions and group projects on this course?
lookingFor: Specific, self-aware sense of what they contribute to a creative cohort, beyond generic enthusiasm.

bullets: Name a specific strength (technical skill, an outside perspective, organizational habit)
Back it with a concrete past example of contributing to a group
Show awareness this is a two-way exchange, not just what they'll take
idealAnswer.modelAnswer: I think I'd bring a fairly blunt, constructive style of feedback, because I ran an informal photo club at school where we critiqued each other's work weekly, and I got good at being specific about what wasn't working rather than just saying 'I like it' or staying silent. I also have some strength in lighting setups from working weekend jobs at a local studio, which I'd be glad to share with classmates who haven't had that access. But I'm also looking forward to being on the other side of it, being around people with different reference points and getting pushed on my own blind spots.

commonMistakes: Vague enthusiasm with no specific skill or habit named
Framing it entirely as what they'll gain rather than contribute
No concrete past example of contributing to a group creative process
followUps: Tell us about a time you gave feedback that someone found genuinely useful.

question: Photography is a competitive field to earn a living in. What's your realistic understanding of that, and how does it affect why you're applying?
lookingFor: Grounded awareness of the industry's difficulty without being either naive or discouraged, and a genuine reason for pursuing it anyway.

bullets: Show honest awareness of the field's competitiveness or income variability
Avoid naive optimism or unearned confidence about 'making it'
Explain what still draws them to it despite the difficulty
idealAnswer.modelAnswer: I've talked to a couple of working photographers, including one who does weddings full-time and one who freelances editorial alongside a part-time job, and both were clear that steady income takes years to build and often means diversifying across genres or adding teaching or retouching work. That's not discouraging to me, it's more that I want to go in with realistic expectations rather than assuming a degree guarantees a career shooting exactly what I love. What keeps me applying anyway is that even hearing the harder parts honestly, neither of them wanted to do anything else, and that's the kind of certainty I want to test in myself too.

commonMistakes: Naive claim that talent alone will guarantee success
So discouraged by the difficulty that motivation seems shaky
No evidence of having actually researched the realities of the industry
followUps: What other skills might you build alongside photography to support that path?

question: If you had to photograph the same ordinary object every day for a month and make each image different, how would you approach it?
lookingFor: Creative problem-solving and technical range, showing they can generate variety from limitation rather than needing novelty handed to them.

bullets: Suggest a range of variables to change (light, angle, lens, context, time of day)
Show awareness that constraint can force creativity rather than limit it
Give a specific, plausible plan rather than a vague 'I'd get creative'
idealAnswer.modelAnswer: I'd deliberately change one variable at a time so the differences are real rather than random, shooting the same object at different times of day to use changing light, then varying focal length and distance, from a macro-style close crop to a wide shot placing it in context. I'd also let its surroundings change it, photographing it in use, in storage, damaged, next to different objects, so the object becomes almost a lens onto everything around it rather than the whole subject. I actually think constraints like this are more useful than free choice, because with infinite options I tend to default to my usual habits, and a strict limitation forces me to solve problems I wouldn't otherwise attempt.

commonMistakes: Vague answer with no specific variables to vary
Treating the constraint as purely limiting rather than generative
Suggesting essentially the same shot repeated with no real differentiation
followUps: Which of those thirty images do you think would end up strongest, and why?

question: Can a single photograph really tell a story, or does it always need context around it?
lookingFor: A thoughtful, opinionated position that engages with the tension between single-image and series-based storytelling.

bullets: Take a genuine position rather than sitting on the fence
Support it with a specific image or example
Acknowledge the counterargument seriously before settling
idealAnswer.modelAnswer: I think a single photograph can suggest a story but rarely tells the whole thing on its own, it usually relies on the viewer bringing assumptions to fill the gaps. A photo of an empty pair of shoes by a doorway implies absence or departure, but that reading depends entirely on captions, context, or cultural assumptions the viewer already holds. I lean toward believing series work is more honest storytelling because it gives you enough frames to build a real arc, though I'll admit some single images, like the famous ones from major historical moments, do carry enough weight and context from being seen so widely that they function almost like a whole story by themselves.

commonMistakes: Refusing to take any position on the question
No specific image or example used to support the argument
Ignoring the role of context, captions, or viewer assumption entirely
followUps: What would a caption add to or take away from one of your own images?

question: Beyond taking the photo itself, what other skills do you think matter for a working photographer, and which do you already have?
lookingFor: Awareness that the craft includes business, communication, and post-production skills, plus honest self-assessment.

bullets: Name skills beyond shooting itself (editing, client communication, self-promotion, organization)
Give an honest self-assessment of strengths and gaps
Show it's not framed as a job pitch, but genuine self-awareness for a student
idealAnswer.modelAnswer: I think editing workflow, client communication, and basic self-promotion matter as much as the shooting itself, because I've seen friends with excellent images struggle simply because they were disorganized about delivering files on time or unclear in emails with clients. I'm fairly confident in my editing, I taught myself a consistent process from my film days for keeping raw files organized, but I know client communication is a weaker area, I tend to under-explain what I'm doing during a shoot, which I'd like to get better at during the course through actual client-facing projects.

commonMistakes: Naming only camera-handling skills as if that's all that matters
Overclaiming competence in every area with no honest gap named
Framing the answer as a professional job pitch rather than student self-reflection
followUps: How would you go about improving the weaker skill you mentioned?

question: How would you describe your photographic style right now, and how do you expect it to change here?
lookingFor: Honest self-assessment of a still-developing style, with realistic expectations that a degree will shape and challenge it.

bullets: Describe their current style with specific, observable traits, not just adjectives
Be honest that it's still forming rather than claiming a fully fixed voice
Show openness to the course challenging or reshaping that style
idealAnswer.modelAnswer: Right now I'd describe my style as quiet and observational, I tend to shoot muted color, natural light, and I gravitate toward in-between moments rather than posed ones, which probably comes from how much documentary work I've been doing. I don't think it's a fully formed voice yet though, it's more a set of habits I've settled into because they're comfortable, and I can already tell from looking at other students' portfolios online that I've barely touched studio lighting or more constructed image-making. I actually want the course to unsettle that comfort a bit, I'd rather leave with a wider range and have to rebuild a style from a stronger foundation than protect what I already do.

commonMistakes: Claiming a fully fixed, mature style with no room to grow
Vague adjectives like 'artistic' or 'unique' with no observable traits
Resistance to the idea that the course might change their style
followUps: What kind of work outside your comfort zone are you most nervous to try?
